title: Sourdough Loaf
intro: A naturally leavened country loaf with a blistered, deep brown crust and an open, tangy crumb, baked in a lidded pot for maximum oven spring.
ingredients: 100 g (½ cup) active sourdough starter, bubbly and fed 4 to 8 hours earlier
375 ml (1½ cups plus 1 tbsp) lukewarm water
450 g (3⅔ cups) strong white bread flour
Rice flour, for dusting the proving basket
steps: Stir the starter into the water in a large bowl until it loosens, then add both flours and mix with your hand until there are no dry patches. Cover and leave for 45 minutes to 1 hour so the flour can hydrate.
Sprinkle the salt over the dough with a splash of water and squeeze and pinch it through until you can no longer feel the grains. Cover again.

Leave the dough to bulk ferment at a warm room temperature, around 24 °C (75 °F), for 4 to 6 hours. For the first 2 hours, give it a set of stretch-and-folds every 30 minutes: lift one edge, stretch it up and fold it over the middle, turn the bowl and repeat four times. It is ready when it has grown by about half, looks domed and jiggles when you shake the bowl.

Tip the dough onto a lightly floured surface and fold it loosely into a round. Leave it uncovered for 20 to 30 minutes, then shape it tightly into a boule or batard, pulling the surface taut, and set it seam-side up in a proving basket dusted with rice flour (or a bowl lined with a well-floured cloth).
Cover the basket with a bag or shower cap and refrigerate for 12 to 16 hours. The cold rest firms the dough for scoring and builds flavour.
Put a lidded cast-iron pot about 24 cm (9½ in) across into the oven and heat it to 250 °C (480 °F, fan 230 °C) for a full 45 minutes to 1 hour.

Turn the cold dough out onto a square of baking parchment, slash the top about 1 cm (½ in) deep with a razor or very sharp knife, and lower it into the hot pot using the parchment. Cover and bake for 20 minutes, then remove the lid, reduce the oven to 230 °C (450 °F, fan 210 °C) and bake for a further 20 to 25 minutes until the crust is deep brown and the loaf sounds hollow when tapped underneath.
Cool on a wire rack for at least 1 hour before cutting; the crumb is still setting as it cools.

title: Croissants
time: About 14 hours, including resting and proving
intro: Classic laminated crescents built from a lean yeasted dough and a slab of cold butter folded three times, baked until they shatter into flaky, honeycombed layers.
ingredients: 500 g (4 cups) strong white bread flour, plus extra for dusting
280 g (1¼ cups) cold unsalted butter, for the butter block
1 egg, beaten with 1 tbsp milk, to glaze
steps: Mix the flour, sugar, salt and yeast in a large bowl, pour in the milk and water and bring together into a dough. Knead for only 3 to 4 minutes, until smooth but not springy, then pat it into a rectangle about 20 x 15 cm (8 x 6 in), wrap and chill for at least 2 hours or overnight.

Make the butter block: lay the cold butter between two sheets of baking parchment and beat and roll it into a 20 x 20 cm (8 x 8 in) square of even thickness. Chill until firm but still bendable, about 15 minutes; the butter and dough should feel similar in firmness when you laminate.
Roll the dough on a floured surface to a 40 x 20 cm (16 x 8 in) rectangle. Set the butter square on one half, fold the bare half over it and pinch the edges closed so the butter is sealed inside.

Roll the parcel away from you into a strip about 60 x 20 cm (24 x 8 in), brushing off loose flour, and fold it in thirds like a letter. This is the first turn. Wrap and chill for 30 minutes, then repeat the rolling and letter fold twice more, chilling 30 minutes between each turn. After the third turn, chill for at least 1 hour or overnight.

Roll the dough to roughly 60 x 25 cm (24 x 10 in) and 4 mm (⅙ in) thick. Trim the edges straight, then cut it into long triangles with a 10 cm (4 in) base. Make a small nick in the centre of each base, gently stretch the triangle, and roll it up from the base to the tip.

Set the croissants on lined baking trays with the tip tucked underneath, well spaced, and curve the ends slightly. Brush lightly with the egg glaze and prove uncovered at about 24 °C (75 °F) for 2 to 3 hours, until doubled and wobbly; keep them cooler than 27 °C (80 °F) or the butter will leak out.

Heat the oven to 200 °C (400 °F, fan 180 °C). Glaze the croissants again and bake for 18 to 20 minutes, swapping the trays halfway, until deeply golden and crisp. Cool on a rack for 10 minutes before eating.

title: Baguette
intro: Slender French loaves with a crackling golden crust and a light, airy crumb, baked on a hot stone with a burst of steam.
ingredients: 500 g (4 cups) strong white bread flour, plus extra for dusting
A little olive oil, for the bowl
Semolina or flour, for the tray or peel
steps: Put the flour in a large bowl with the salt on one side and the yeast on the other, add the water and mix to a soft, slightly sticky dough. Knead on an unfloured surface for about 10 minutes (or 6 to 7 minutes with a dough hook) until smooth and stretchy, then place in a lightly oiled bowl and cover.

Let the dough rise at room temperature for 1 to 1½ hours until doubled. For a deeper flavour, give it 15 minutes at room temperature and then refrigerate for 12 to 24 hours instead, letting it come back to room temperature before shaping.

Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and divide it into three pieces of about 280 g (10 oz). Pat each into a rough rectangle, roll it loosely into a log and rest for 15 minutes under a cloth.

Shape each log: flatten it gently, fold the top third down and press, fold the bottom third up and press, then fold in half lengthways and seal the seam with the heel of your hand. Roll it back and forth to a 35 cm (14 in) length, tapering the ends.
Lay the baguettes seam-side down in the folds of a well-floured cloth or on a tray dusted with semolina, cover loosely and prove for 45 minutes to 1 hour until puffy but still springy to the touch.
Meanwhile, heat the oven to 240 °C (475 °F, fan 220 °C) with a baking stone or heavy baking tray on the middle shelf and an empty roasting tin on the shelf below.

Transfer the baguettes to a peel or a sheet of baking parchment and make 3 or 4 overlapping diagonal slashes along each with a razor held at a shallow angle. Slide them onto the hot stone, pour about 250 ml (1 cup) of hot water into the roasting tin for steam and close the door at once. Bake for 20 to 25 minutes until deep golden and hollow-sounding, then cool on a rack for at least 20 minutes.

title: Japanese Milk Bread
intro: A pillowy, feathery white loaf made with a cooked flour-and-milk paste, the tangzhong, which keeps the crumb soft and springy for days.
ingredients: 25 g (3 tbsp) strong white bread flour, for the tangzhong
125 ml (½ cup) whole milk, for the tangzhong
325 g (2⅔ cups) strong white bread flour
40 g (3 tbsp) unsalted butter, softened and cubed
1 egg yolk beaten with 1 tbsp milk, to glaze
steps: Make the tangzhong: whisk the 25 g flour and 125 ml milk together in a small pan until lump-free, then cook over medium heat, stirring constantly, for 2 to 3 minutes until it thickens to a paste that holds the lines of the whisk, about 65 °C (150 °F). Scrape into a bowl, press cling film onto the surface and cool to room temperature.

Put the remaining flour, the sugar, salt and yeast into the bowl of a stand mixer. Add the cooled tangzhong, the lukewarm milk and the egg and mix with the dough hook on low for 2 minutes, then on medium for 5 minutes until the dough gathers around the hook.

Add the butter a few cubes at a time and keep kneading for 8 to 10 minutes until the dough is smooth, glossy and can be stretched thin enough to see light through without tearing. By hand this takes 15 to 20 minutes of slapping and folding.
Shape the dough into a ball, return it to the bowl, cover and leave to rise for 1 to 1½ hours until doubled.

Grease a 23 x 13 cm (9 x 5 in) loaf tin. Press the air out of the dough, divide it into three equal pieces and round each one. Roll a piece into an oval about 20 cm (8 in) long, fold the long sides into the middle, then roll it up tightly from a short end. Repeat with the others and set the three rolls side by side in the tin, seams down.
Cover loosely and prove for 45 minutes to 1 hour until the dough domes about 1 cm (½ in) above the rim of the tin.

Heat the oven to 180 °C (350 °F, fan 160 °C). Brush the top gently with the glaze and bake for 30 to 35 minutes until deep golden and the centre reads about 90 °C (195 °F) on a thermometer; tent with foil after 20 minutes if it is browning too fast.
Leave in the tin for 10 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack and cool completely before slicing so the crumb does not compress.

title: Dan Dan Noodles
intro: Sichuan street noodles with a numbing, fiery sesame and chilli-oil sauce hiding at the bottom of the bowl, topped with crisp fried pork and preserved greens.
ingredients: 400 g (14 oz) fresh thin wheat noodles, or 300 g (10½ oz) dried
1 tbsp dark soy sauce, for the pork
2 tbsp sui mi ya cai (Sichuan preserved mustard greens), or finely chopped pickled mustard greens
4 tbsp Chinese sesame paste or tahini
4 tbsp chilli oil with its sediment, or to taste
200 ml (¾ cup) hot noodle-cooking water or chicken stock
steps: Make the sauce: stir the sesame paste with the light soy sauce, vinegar and sugar until smooth, then mix in the chilli oil, Sichuan pepper and garlic. It will be thick; that is fine for now.

Heat the oil in a wok over high heat, add the pork and fry, breaking it up, for 4 to 5 minutes until browned and crisp at the edges. Splash in the rice wine and dark soy sauce and stir until the liquid has cooked away, then add the ya cai and stir-fry for 1 minute more. Take off the heat.
Bring a large pot of water to the boil and cook the noodles until just tender, 2 to 3 minutes for fresh or as the packet directs for dried. Drain, keeping back a cupful of the cooking water.
Divide the sauce between four deep bowls and loosen each with about 3 tablespoons of the hot cooking water or stock, stirring until it is pourable.
Pile the noodles on top of the sauce, spoon over the pork, and finish with spring onions and peanuts. Toss everything together at the table just before eating.

title: Udon Soup with Tempura Shrimp
intro: Thick, chewy udon in a clear dashi broth seasoned with soy and mirin, crowned with lacy, crisp tempura shrimp.
ingredients: 2 portions frozen or fresh udon noodles, about 500 g (1 lb 2 oz)
1 litre (4 cups) dashi stock, made from kombu and bonito flakes or instant dashi powder
8 large raw shrimp (prawns), peeled with tails left on, deveined
80 g (⅔ cup) plain flour, plus extra for dusting
180 ml (¾ cup) ice-cold sparkling or still water
steps: Make 3 or 4 shallow cuts across the underside of each shrimp and press down gently along its back to straighten it so it stays flat when fried. Pat dry and keep cold.
Bring the dashi, soy sauce, mirin, sugar and salt to a gentle simmer in a pan, taste for seasoning and keep warm over the lowest heat.

Pour about 5 cm (2 in) of oil into a deep pan and heat to 180 °C (350 °F). Only when the oil is ready, whisk the egg yolk into the iced water, tip in the flour and cornflour and stir briefly with chopsticks; a lumpy, barely mixed batter gives the lightest coating.

Dust the shrimp with flour, hold each by the tail, dip into the batter and lower into the oil. Fry four at a time for 2 to 3 minutes until the coating is pale gold and crisp, then drain on a wire rack.
Cook the udon in a large pot of boiling water for 1 to 2 minutes for frozen (or as the packet directs) until the strands loosen and are hot through, then drain well.
Divide the noodles between two deep bowls, ladle over the hot broth and top with the tempura shrimp, spring onions and a pinch of togarashi. Serve straight away while the tempura is still crisp.

title: Tonkatsu
intro: Juicy pork loin cutlets in a shaggy, golden panko crust, sliced and served with shredded cabbage, rice and a tangy fruity sauce.
ingredients: 4 boneless pork loin chops, about 2 cm (¾ in) thick and 150 g (5 oz) each
¼ white cabbage, very finely shredded
Tonkatsu sauce, bought or made by mixing 4 tbsp ketchup, 2 tbsp Worcestershire sauce, 1 tbsp soy sauce and 1 tsp sugar
Steamed rice and lemon wedges, to serve
steps: Make small cuts through the band of fat and sinew around the edge of each chop every 2 cm (¾ in) so it does not curl, then pound lightly to an even thickness of about 1.5 cm (⅝ in). Season both sides with salt and pepper.

Set out three shallow dishes with the flour, the beaten egg and the panko. Coat each chop in flour, shake off the excess, dip in egg, then press firmly into the panko on both sides so it is thickly covered. Rest for 5 minutes so the coating sets.

Heat about 3 cm (1¼ in) of oil in a wide, heavy pan to 170 °C (340 °F). Fry two chops at a time for 3 to 4 minutes per side until deep golden and a thermometer in the centre reads 63 °C (145 °F). Drain on a wire rack for 3 minutes.
While the pork fries, drop the shredded cabbage into iced water for 5 minutes to crisp it, then drain and dry it well.
Cut each cutlet across into strips about 2 cm (¾ in) wide and serve with the cabbage, rice, lemon wedges and plenty of sauce.

title: Char Siu
intro: Cantonese barbecued pork, marinated in hoisin, soy, honey and five-spice, then roasted and glazed until the edges turn sticky and charred.
ingredients: 1 kg (2¼ lb) boneless pork shoulder or pork neck, cut into strips about 4 cm (1½ in) thick
3 tbsp honey, plus 2 tbsp for the glaze
2 cubes fermented red bean curd, mashed, or ½ tsp red food colouring (optional, for colour)
steps: Stir together the hoisin, both soy sauces, rice wine, 3 tablespoons of honey, the sugar, bean curd, five-spice, garlic, sesame oil and white pepper. Spoon 3 tablespoons into a small bowl and refrigerate for glazing. Coat the pork in the rest in a bag or container and marinate in the fridge overnight, or for at least 4 hours, turning once.

Heat the oven to 200 °C (400 °F, fan 180 °C). Line a roasting tin with foil, pour in about 1 cm (½ in) of water to catch drips and set a wire rack over it. Lift the pork out of the marinade, let the excess drip off and lay the strips on the rack.
Roast for 25 minutes, turn the strips over and roast for another 15 minutes.

Warm the reserved marinade with the remaining 2 tablespoons of honey until runny. Brush the pork all over, turn the oven up to 230 °C (450 °F, fan 210 °C) and roast for 5 to 8 minutes more, brushing once again, until the edges are glossy and charred in spots and the centre reads 70 °C (160 °F).
Rest the pork for 10 minutes, then slice across the grain and serve with steamed rice and any leftover glaze spooned over.

title: Braised Pork Belly, hong shao rou
intro: Cubes of pork belly caramelised in sugar and slowly braised with soy, rice wine and star anise until meltingly soft and lacquered red, with hard-boiled eggs soaking up the sauce.
ingredients: 800 g (1¾ lb) skin-on pork belly, cut into 3 cm (1¼ in) cubes
40 g (3 tbsp) rock sugar or granulated sugar
3 spring onions, cut into 5 cm (2 in) lengths
500 ml (2 cups) hot water, or enough to just cover
steps: Put the pork in a pot, cover with cold water, bring to the boil and simmer for 3 minutes, then drain, rinse and pat dry. Meanwhile boil the eggs for 8 minutes, cool them in cold water and peel.

Heat the oil and sugar together in a wok or heavy casserole over medium-low heat, stirring, for 3 to 5 minutes until the sugar melts and turns amber. Add the pork and toss it in the caramel for 2 to 3 minutes until the edges colour, standing back because it will spit.
Add the ginger, spring onions, star anise, cinnamon and chillies and stir for 1 minute. Pour in the rice wine, both soy sauces and enough hot water to just cover the meat, and bring to the boil.
Cover, turn the heat right down and simmer gently for 1 hour until the pork is tender. Add the peeled eggs for the last 30 minutes, turning them once so they colour evenly.
Remove the lid, raise the heat and let the sauce bubble for 10 to 15 minutes, spooning it over the pork, until it is thick and glossy. Fish out the whole spices and serve with rice.

title: Herb-Crusted Rack of Lamb
intro: Seared racks of lamb painted with Dijon mustard and pressed into a green crust of breadcrumbs, garlic and herbs, roasted until rosy pink.
ingredients: 2 racks of lamb, French-trimmed, 7 to 8 ribs each, about 700 g (1½ lb) each
steps: Take the lamb out of the fridge 30 minutes before cooking and heat the oven to 200 °C (400 °F, fan 180 °C). Pat the racks dry, score the fat lightly in a diamond pattern and season well all over.

Heat the oil in a large ovenproof frying pan over high heat and sear the racks fat-side down for 3 to 4 minutes until golden, then brown the ends and the meaty side for about 1 minute each. Move them to a board and let them cool for 5 minutes.
Mix the breadcrumbs with the garlic, parsley, rosemary, thyme, lemon zest, melted butter and a pinch of salt and pepper until the crumbs are evenly damp.

Brush the meaty side of each rack with mustard and press the crumb mixture firmly onto it to make an even crust. Set the racks crust-side up in a roasting tin, interlocking the bones if you like, and wrap the exposed bone tips in foil to stop them scorching.

Roast for 18 to 22 minutes for medium-rare, when a thermometer in the thickest part reads 55 °C (130 °F), or about 25 minutes for medium at 60 °C (140 °F). Cover loosely with foil if the crust darkens too quickly.
Rest the racks under foil for 10 minutes, then carve between the bones into cutlets and serve 3 or 4 per person.

title: Grilled Lamb Chops
intro: Lamb chops marinated in lemon, garlic, rosemary and cumin, charred over high heat and served with a cooling mint yogurt.
ingredients: 8 lamb loin chops or 12 rib chops, about 2.5 cm (1 in) thick
2 tsp chopped fresh oregano, or 1 tsp dried
steps: Whisk the oil with the garlic, rosemary, oregano, lemon zest, half the lemon juice, the cumin, 1 teaspoon of salt and plenty of pepper. Turn the chops in the marinade and leave for 1 hour at room temperature, or up to 24 hours in the fridge, bringing them out 30 minutes before cooking.
Stir the yogurt with the mint, the remaining lemon juice and a pinch of salt, and chill until needed.
Heat a barbecue or a ridged grill pan until very hot, about 230 °C (450 °F). Scrape most of the marinade off the chops so it does not burn, and oil the grates lightly.

Grill the chops for 3 to 4 minutes per side for medium-rare, or until a thermometer reads 55 to 57 °C (130 to 135 °F); give them 1 minute more per side for medium. Stand loin chops on their fat edge for a final minute so the fat crisps.
Rest the chops for 5 minutes loosely covered with foil, then serve with the mint yogurt and lemon wedges.

title: Lamb Curry
intro: Slow-cooked lamb shoulder in a thick, deeply spiced gravy of browned onions, tomato, ginger, garlic and yogurt.
ingredients: 1 kg (2¼ lb) boneless lamb shoulder, cut into 4 cm (1½ in) chunks
1 cinnamon stick, 4 green cardamom pods and 2 bay leaves
Small handful fresh coriander, chopped, to serve
steps: Mix the lamb with the yogurt, half the ginger and garlic, the turmeric and 1 teaspoon of salt. Leave to marinate for 30 minutes, or overnight in the fridge.

Heat the oil in a heavy casserole over medium heat, add the cinnamon, cardamom and bay leaves and let them sizzle for 30 seconds. Add the onions and cook, stirring often, for 15 to 20 minutes until deep golden brown.

Stir in the remaining ginger and garlic for 1 minute, then the ground coriander, cumin and chilli powder for 30 seconds. Tip in the tomatoes and cook for 5 minutes, stirring, until the mixture thickens and oil begins to separate at the edges.
Add the lamb with all its marinade, turn the heat up and stir for 5 minutes until the meat loses its pink colour. Pour in 250 ml (1 cup) of hot water and bring to the boil.
Cover and simmer very gently for about 1½ hours, stirring now and then and adding a splash of water if it looks dry, until the lamb is fork-tender.
Uncover and simmer for 10 minutes more to thicken the gravy, then stir in the garam masala, check the salt and scatter with fresh coriander. Serve with rice or flatbreads.

title: Lamb Tagine with Apricots
intro: A slow Moroccan stew of lamb shoulder with cumin, cinnamon and saffron, sweetened at the end with dried apricots and honey and finished with toasted almonds.
ingredients: 1.2 kg (2½ lb) boneless lamb shoulder, cut into 4 cm (1½ in) chunks
2 tsp each ground cumin and ground coriander
1 tsp ground cinnamon, 1 tsp sweet paprika and ½ tsp ground turmeric
Pinch of saffron threads, soaked in 2 tbsp warm water
500 ml (2 cups) chicken or lamb stock
Fresh coriander leaves and couscous, to serve
steps: Season the lamb well. Heat the oil in a tagine or heavy casserole over medium-high heat and brown the meat in batches for 3 to 4 minutes each, without crowding the pan, then set it aside.
Lower the heat, add the onions and cook for 8 minutes until soft. Stir in the garlic, ginger and all the ground spices and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Return the lamb and any juices to the pot, add the tomatoes, stock and saffron with its soaking water, and bring to a simmer.
Cover and cook over the lowest heat, or in the oven at 160 °C (325 °F, fan 140 °C), for 1½ hours until the lamb is tender.
Stir in the apricots and honey and simmer uncovered for a further 30 minutes until the sauce thickens and the apricots are plump. Season to taste.
Scatter with the toasted almonds and coriander leaves and serve with couscous.
